title: Astronomers Discover First Green Star After It Devours Its Own Planets – Gizmodo Breakthrough
body:
Astronomers have identified the first known “green” star—a white dwarf that glows with a vivid emerald hue after devouring the remnants of its own planetary system. The discovery, made using spectroscopic data from the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope, reveals that the star’s atmosphere is enriched with heavy elements such as magnesium, calcium and iron, which scatter light in a way that produces the unusual coloration. The finding not only expands the known palette of stellar colors but also provides a rare glimpse into the violent final act of planetary death and rebirth in the cosmos.

White dwarfs are the dense, cooling cores left behind when Sun‑like stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and shed their outer layers. Typically, these stellar embers appear white or bluish, their light dominated by the high temperatures of their surfaces. However, when a white dwarf’s intense gravity pulls in debris from disintegrated planets, asteroids or comets, the infalling material can “pollute” its atmosphere with heavier elements that would otherwise sink beneath the surface. In the newly observed object—designated WD J1243+1620—astronomers detected a striking excess of magnesium and calcium, elements known to reflect green wavelengths more efficiently than the usual hydrogen and helium that dominate white dwarf spectra. This combination creates a spectral signature that translates to a greenish tint when rendered in visible light.

The phenomenon was first flagged by a team led by Dr. Elena Marquez of the Institute for Astrophysics in Madrid, who noticed an anomalous bump in the star’s spectral curve while surveying a catalog of nearby white dwarfs. Follow‑up observations confirmed that the bump corresponded to a strong Mg I triplet, a set of absorption lines that, when broadened by the star’s high pressure, scatter green light preferentially. “It’s like the star is wearing a green coat made of planetary ashes,” Marquez said in a press briefing. “We are essentially watching the aftermath of a planetary system being ripped apart and its material being re‑processed in the star’s outer layers.”

The discovery has broader implications for our understanding of planetary system evolution. Studies over the past decade have shown that a significant fraction of white dwarfs exhibit signs of metal pollution, implying that many planetary systems survive their host star’s red‑giant phase only to be destabilized later. The green hue of WD J1243+1620 offers a visual confirmation of this process and suggests that the composition of the engulfed bodies can vary widely. If the star has accreted a planet rich in magnesium—perhaps a rocky world akin to Earth’s mantle—the resulting spectral fingerprint would differ from that of a star that has swallowed a more iron‑rich or carbon‑rich planet. By cataloguing such variations, astronomers hope to reconstruct the chemical makeup of exoplanetary material that is otherwise impossible to observe directly.

The finding also challenges long‑standing assumptions about the limits of stellar coloration. While the colors of main‑sequence stars are dictated primarily by surface temperature, the colors of compact remnants like white dwarfs can be altered by external factors such as accreted debris. This opens the door to a more nuanced taxonomy of stellar colors, where “green” is no longer a mythic rarity but a possible outcome of planetary consumption. Future surveys with next‑generation instruments, including the James Webb Space Telescope and the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope, are expected to identify additional anomalously colored white dwarfs, refining models of how planetary material is redistributed after a star’s death.

As researchers continue to analyze the spectrum of WD J1243+1620, they aim to determine the exact mass and composition of the ingested planetary fragments, and to estimate how long the green phase will persist before the star cools and the metals settle beneath its photosphere. The discovery underscores the dynamic and often violent interplay between stars and their planets, reminding us that even in death, stars can produce spectacular, unexpected displays. With each new observation, the cosmos reveals another shade of its complex story—one that may soon include more green, pink, or purple remnants, expanding our visual and scientific understanding of the universe’s final chapters.
